site.aboutText: I design and engineer practical systems, tooling, and products. This portfolio is organized by discipline and each section contains documented examples of my work.

about.heading: About
about.name: Branson Murdock
paragraphs: I grew up making short films and VFX shorts, and that early experience with visual storytelling shaped the way I think about design. From there, I moved into graphic design, where I learned how to communicate ideas clearly and thoughtfully. Over time, I became drawn to work that could have a more tangible impact on the real world, so I redirected that creative energy into engineering. I enjoy working hands-on and finding solutions in manufacturing and product design that improve both how products are made and how people use them.

I see myself as a multidisciplinary engineer and a bit of a jack of all trades, someone who likes to bring together different perspectives, skills, and life experiences to solve problems in creative ways. I’m always looking for ways to make processes faster and more efficient, whether that means improving the way I work or helping the people around me work more effectively. I’m especially interested in work that sits at the intersection of design, fabrication, and practical implementation, whether that means programming, hardware design, plastics, metalworking, woodworking, or building things just to learn and experiment. In my free time, I’m often outdoors or deep in personal projects that explore new mediums, tools, and ideas.
about.location: Open to work in the U.S.

sections.title: Automation / Digital Transformation
sections.summary: A collection of the systems I built to make production easier to see, understand, and react to, from PLC logic and line signals to custom SCADA screens and production data.

detailGroups.title: Beckhoff Control Enclosure Design
description: I designed this control enclosure for a smaller project that did not need much IO yet. So for the moment it is just a bare bones way of providing power to the Beckhoff IPC for testing purposes

The purpose for this controls enclosure was to provide a server testing environment for testing a custom Scada system that I built in house while still keeping the system open to more PLC expansion at a later time.

detailGroups.title: Live Automated Line Signals
description: This was a the physical shop floor visibility extension for our Scada system. I programmed this as part of an Andon signal-for-help system so an issue on the line could be seen and acted on before it quietly became a larger delay.
The Scada system would write values to a database, a Beckhoff connected to these lights would read from that database and tell which lights to turn on based on different statuses.
This was programmed using TwinCat. The program was  in such as way that as more light sequences or status indicators are added the logic can be easily adjusted.

detailGroups.title: Scada System Design
description: I designed this custom SCADA system from the ground up. It is built on a Python (Flask) backend with a traditional HTML,CSS,Javascript frontend. The advantage of building a scada system this way is that there unlike some popular Scada systems there are no steep licensing fees and using a modern web frame work enabled a lot more for the business use cases.
Because this framework was so flexible and easily expandable, I was able to digitalize and make multiple process faster and easier to access for end users.

detailGroups.title: Scada System Design
description: Building a production scheduler into the Scada system was a natural fit. From here managers with the proper rights are able to go in and schedule what units they are building and during what times.
That data would then be fed into our database which the Scada system, using ADS communication, would tell the Beckhoff IPC driving the production lights to go and read the new production schedule.
From there the physical production lights would be in sync with the scada system for things like indicating line move times, break times, etc.

detailGroups.title: Scada System Dashboard Integration
description: This dashboard was designed so that anyone on the production line could glance up at the TV and see how much time they had left to complete their current unit. It acted as the drum beat for the production line. As well as operators seeing this team leads and other managers could also see if a station was behind schedule and address any problems.

Before I implemented this system there was no visibility to how many units had been completed at any given point in time and there was no way to know if the production line was on track to finish for the day.

detailGroups.title: Scada System Design
description: Andon Requests are made in the Scada system which was made available to all operators and managers on the production line.
These requests tie directly into the production lights and the production dashboard so that anyone on the line can see that a request has been made and what type of request it is.

When a product has been found in production that is non forming to specifications it can immediately be tagged in this system as well which automatically prints a red tag label and adds it to a queue system for the quality team to address.

sections.title: Building Infrastructure
sections.summary: The physical side of the work: rearranging stations, building material-handling equipment, and fitting new infrastructure into a working production space.

detailGroups.title: Pallet Conveyor Build
description: I designed and built this pallet conveyor in-house to move product through the line without buying a system that was more complicated or expensive than we needed. Keeping it modular also made it easier to adapt the layout as the process changed.
Building it in house provided cost savings of $20,000+ especially since as they want to build more they now have the design files and can easily expand at a low cost.

This also allowed us to implement a kanban system for critical components that are harder to restock. The conveyor is designed to be easy to load and unload, and the modular design allows us to add or remove sections as needed.

detailGroups.title: Material Handling Carts
description: These carts were designed and built in-house to move product through the fabrication processes without buying a system that was more complicated or expensive than we needed.

detailGroups.title: Process Flow Reorder
description: I wanted a quick way to try new station layouts without spending the time to rebuild the entire area in CAD first.

I 3D-scanned the station as it existed, brought that scan into Blender, and rearranged the components there. That gave me a believable starting point and let me test the process flow before moving anything in the real space.

This ended up being much faster than recreating the station from scratch in CAD, and the scan kept the layout honest because it included all the awkward real-world details that are easy to leave out of a clean model.

detailGroups.title: Weld Area Layout / Work Cell Design
description: I laid out the weld area as a set of modular work cells so the process could change without making the entire space obsolete. The goal was to keep parts moving in a sensible direction, reduce unnecessary handling, and give each welder a safe and standardized workspace with proper ventilation in each weld booth.

detailGroups.title: Bridge Crane Integration
description: While helping to expand our facilities I was tasked with designing a free standing bridge crane design that would be able to lift and move large products on the production line. It also needed to be able to be configured on site without requiring any more equipment than a forklift and a few people to assemble it.

I designed the system so that we could reuse the design to span variable distances just by varying the length of cut square tubing. By doing this we were able to reuse this design for two different areas in the facility.
To ensure safety I did stress analysis on the design to ensure that the crane would be able to lift the required loads without any risk of failure.

detailGroups.title: Jib Crane Integration
description: As part of the facilities expansion, We had a couple of existing Jib cranes that we wanted to move to the new location as well as fabricate a couple more.
Since we didn't have the original designs I reverse engineered the existing cranes and designed a new one to match the existing ones.
To make the existing crane fit our new operations I also designed a riser base that would allow the crane to be mounted higher and give us more clearance for our operations.
I also did stress analysis on all the designs to ensure that it would be able to lift the required loads without any risk of failure.

detailGroups.title: Powder Coat Infrastructure
description: I help with a couple of different projects to improve our powder coat area. This included designing and building new ceiling ventilation fans to improve the airflow in the area as well as a wash trough drip catch pan to catch any excess water that would drip off the parts after they were washed and before they were powder coated.
The ventilation fans were designed to be installed in place of existing sky lights using the same roof hole opening. They were also designed to be easily accessible for maintenance and cleaning.

sections.title: Personal Projects
sections.summary: A collection of personal projects that I have worked on in my free time. These projects are a mix of metalworking, plastics and composites, woodworking, and other projects that I have taken on to learn new skills and challenge myself.

detailGroups.title: Wood Work Bench
description: While coming up with the design for this work bench I was inspired by old roman and english woodworking benches and techniques. I wanted something that was simple and designed around the intent to be used with hand tools (handsaws, hand planes, chisels, etc.).

Also something that was important to me with this design was that everything be assembled using traditional woodworking joinery techniques and not using any screws or nails. This was a challenge to build but I am happy with the end result.

I also built this all while in our two room apartment with no garage or shop space and in the middle of the winter (so not much to be done outside). So I had to be creative with how I built this. My old landlord would get a kick out of the hand plane shavings all over the floor

detailGroups.title: Van Swivel Seat
description: This is a personal project where I built a swivel seat mechanism for my van. This was more of a reverse engineering challenge to see how cheap I could make something that would have otherwise cost me about $300 (not so practical on my student budget).

This design uses a trailer wheel bearing assembly and spring locking mechanism. I only had two product images to work from (of the original product). Also the locking mechanism wasn't visible in the product images so I had to figure out how it worked and how to make it work with my design.

detailGroups.title: Van Swivel Seat
description: This is my favorite position to put the seat in. Which is more or less a happy accident as I didn't even think about this when I was looking into these swivel seats.
I just get to put my feet up and relax as I look at the stars above. The next best thing without having to cut a hole in the roof of the van to install a sun roof.

detailGroups.title: Ski Board
description: This was part of a plastics and composites class where I was able to practice wet layup.

The ski was built using fiberglass, epoxy resin, and carbon fiber (for the top decal), and a wooden core, allowing me to experiment with different layering techniques and achieve a strong, lightweight structure.

Having never seen skis built before or never seeing what the inside of a ski looks like, I had to do a lot of research and reverse engineering to figure out how to build this ski. I was able to find some information on the internet about how skis are built and what materials are used, but I had to experiment with different techniques and materials to achieve the desired result.

detailGroups.title: Free Ski (Free Skate Ski)
description: While making my ski boards I also wanted to experiment with trying to make one of my favorite hobbies, Free Skating, work in the snow.

Others have done this successfully with ice skates and Free Skates. But I wanted to see if I could apply this same skating technique to snow. So I made a ski board that is similar to a Free Skate but with a ski base and edges. These would be mounted to an aluminum riser that would be attached to snowboard bindings.

I took this out to my local ski hill and just as I supposed. They sunk straight into the snow and I was not able to skate on them. So I will have to try again with a different design that has a larger surface area and more floatation.

detailGroups.title: Motorcycle Trailer
description: This was a project I took on to practice my welding skills and to hopefully in the end have a trailer that I could use to haul my motorcycle around.
I was lucky enough that my work was discontinuing a bunch of trailer frames. So I would need to make some modifications to the frame to make it work for my motorcycle.

A primary part of this design was the wheel chock that would hold the front wheel of the motorcycle in place. I designed this to be adjustable to accommodate different wheel sizes and to ensure a secure fit. I also wanted this to be a quick release design so that I could easily load and unload my motorcycle without having to finick around with trying to keep the motorcycle upright while adding straps and tie downs on the handlebars.

The end result is a trailer that is self contained with ramps and everything so I can just load my motorcycle and go. I can also use this trailer to haul other things around as well which is actually what I have been using it for lately.

And as with most of my personal projects. This was done while I was in school and trying to save money the best I could. So I would have used steel railing and expanded sheet metal for the flooring if I could. But wood was a lot cheaper at the time. So there may be future modifications to this trailer to make it more durable and long lasting. But for now it works great and I am happy with the end result.
And yes that is a Honda XL500R for all you enthusiasts out there. It was my dad's bike back in the day so some might say I have a family heirloom in my possession.

detailGroups.title: Arbor Swing / Day Bed
description: While spending the summer in my hometown I wanted to build something for my wife. My grandparents had some old barn wood laying around. My wife loves porch sitting/swings. So the pieces just fell together after that and I built an arbor swing and day bed for her.

I love modular design as can be seen in a lot of my work. And this is no different. The back rest is adjustable to different lengths so it can be a normal swing or be put all the way back to be a day bed. The swing is also designed to be able to be taken down and stored away if needed. And I designed it in mind that the removable cushion / foldable mattress could slide underneath backrest and be used as a seat pad or mattress for the bed.

All the wood is sealed with polyurethane to protect it from the elements and the rope is a thick braided nylon rope that can withstand the weather. And as with a lot of my projects I used what hardware I had laying around to build this. The sheet metal brackets were made from scrap laying around and the bolts and nuts were from misc farm equipment that my grandpa had laying around.
And I would be amiss if I didn't mention the solar powered "twinkly lights" that my wife is so fond of that we hung so it would be lit up during the night.

sections.title: Product Design
sections.summary: A collection of products I designed and built, from concept to prototype to final product.

detailGroups.title: Van Bed Concept
description: I bought an Astrovan and from the start I knew that the capstone of the build would be a bed that could convert from a couch to a bed and back again. I wanted to make sure that the design was functional, comfortable, and easy to use. I also wanted to make sure that the design was modular and could be easily disassembled and reassembled if needed.

I also knew I wanted storage space underneath the bed for all the gear and cooking infrastructure I would be taking on trips. So I designed the bed to have a storage area underneath that could be accessed from the back and inside the van.

detailGroups.title: Van Bed Build
description: The whole frame structure was designed to be fabricated using solely sheet metal and sheet metal fabrication processes (laser cutting, bending, and welding).
I built my frame out of steel for cost reasons but if I had a larger budget I would have built it out of aluminum to save weight.

detailGroups.title: Van Bed Prototype
description: I powder coated the frame white for a clean esthetic and durable finish. And also added wood in the drawer system to save on weight and I likes the look of the wood as well as an accent to the white powder coated frame.

The bed was made by cutting up a foam mattress into sections and covering them with upholstery fabric. To also increase the utilitarian value the van can still be used to haul cargo inside just by laying the frame in the flat bed position and removing the mattress sections (they are secured by velcro).

detailGroups.title: Moto Tail Bag
description: I love the look and feel of leather and wanted to make a bag that would double as a good medium sized duffle bag as well as tail bag for my motorcycle. I wanted a roll top back to accomodate different sizes of loads.
To keep the design modular and simple I added loop hooks strapping on the sides of the bag to allow for different mounting options and hardware to be attached.
I chose a softer chap leather for the main construction and a harder tooling leather for the straps and accents.

detailGroups.title: Capstone Lifting Mechanism
description: As part of a team, I helped redesign the lifting mechanism for an off-grid construction-site energy system. We changed the solar panel tilting design so the array could make better use of the available sun instead of accepting the limitations of the original setup.

The redesign was not only about getting more angle. We also needed the lift to be more reliable and put less stress into the structure while it moved, so I had to balance the performance improvement with the realities of building and operating it in the field.

sections.title: Tooling And Fixtures
sections.summary: Fixtures and shop-built tools that make parts easier to locate, clamp, weld, drill, and move without asking the operator to solve the same problem from scratch every time.

detailGroups.title: Weld Fixture
detailGroups.description: This weld fixture was designed to hold parts in place in a repeatable way. It was designed with hole locator pins and push pull clamps to make it easy to locate and clamp the parts in place.

detailGroups.title: Weld Fixture Adjustable
description: We found that a fixture does not always need to be permanently fixed. Making the parts adjustable and modular means a worn component can be swapped out, and a revised part does not require rebuilding the whole fixture.

This version uses 8020 aluminum extrusion so I could move and reconfigure the locating points as needed. It also has a practical advantage on the weld floor: spatter is less likely to stick to the extrusion rail and turn the fixture into a cleanup project.

detailGroups.title: Work Holding Fixtures
detailGroups.description: These work-holding fixtures were made for the moments when a part needs to stay put while someone is working on the parts or assembling them together. They each are designed to assist with specific operations to make manual operations faster and more repeatable.

detailGroups.title: Drill Jig
description: Before I implemented this drill fixture there were many safety concerns as well as quality concerns for the way we were performing these drilling operations.
This design addresses all those problems while cutting the time it took to perform those same operations by more than half.

detailGroups.title: Material Movement
detailGroups.description: These fixtures came from the less glamorous but very real problem of moving parts around the workshop without damaging them or making someone fight the load.
